3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1 who filed a written statement contending inter alia that Ramjan Ali and Kader Haji the predecessors of the defendant had occupancy raryati right in the disputed lands and they had been recorded as such in the C.S. Katian. They denied that they were mere bargadars and had no tenancy right and that they did give up possession of the lands to Lal Mia and his brothers. 

 4. Both the Courts below held that Ramjan Ali and kader Haji who had been recorded a well as occupancy raiyats in respect of the disputed land had no right of tenancy therein and that the plaintiff’s had been in possession of the disputed land on the basis of title acquired by their predecessors by means of purchase and settlement and they had been dispossessed by the principal defendants from the said land. 

 5. Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellants, contends that the judgment is bad in law because the Courts below have failed to attach any presumptive value to the record-of-rights which shows that the plaintiff’s predecessors had occupancy right in respect of the disputed lands and that there is no proper finding as to the date of dispossession being within 12 years from the date of institution of the suit. The learned Advocate has further contended that the recitals in deeds, Exts. 1 series and Ext. 2 are not admissible in evidence against the defendants for the purpose of disproving the defendant’s right of tenancy. 

 6. Mr. Ahmad Sobhan, on the other hand, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff, respondents, submits that the Courts below were correct in holding that the entries in the record of rights showing that the defendant’s predecessors were bargadars as well said records did not raise any presumption in favour of the defendant’s. Secondly, even if there was any such presumption, that has been sufficiently rebutted by the documentary and oral evidence that has been adduced in this case. Thirdly, Mr. Sobhan contends, even if the position that the defendant’s predecessors had the right of tenancy in respect of the disputed land is accepted to be true; the evidence of possession which has been brought on record in this case is sufficient to show that the plaintiff’s had been in possession of the disputed land for more than 12 years and as such any right which might have been acquired by them has been determined by such long possession. 

 7. The relevant records-of-right relate to khatian No. 80 and khatian No. 83 of Mouza Galim Khan which have been marked as Ext. 3 and Ext. A respectively Ext. 3 being in respect of khattan 80 of Mouza Galim khan purports to record the superior interest whereas Ext. A. which is in respect of khatian 83, purports to record in interest subordinate to khatian 80. In khatian 83, subordinate to khatian 80. In khatian Kader Haji have been recorded as বর্গা রায়ত স্থিতিবান in the column for the class of interest and in the column of rent, it is recorded “শয্যের জর্দ্ধেক” in the column of superior “খাজনা শামিল” and in the column of superior interest. “খতিয়ান ৮০ আবদুল আজিজ গং” In khatian 80, i. e. Ext. 3 Abdul Aziz and his 5 brothers have been recorded a owners but there is no entry to indicate their status, that is to say, whether they were raiyats or tenure holders and in the column for subordinate interest, khatian 81-84 have been mentioned. Exts. 1 to 1 (b) are three kabalas executed by Abdul Aziz and others, the recorded owners in Ext. 3 in favour of the predecessors of the present plaintiffs and Ext. 2 has been described as a “বেমেয়াদি রায়তি পাট্র।” executed by the same recorded owners in favour of the predecessors of the present plaintiffs. While considering the records-or-rights, both the Courts below have taken the view that the entries in Ext. A showing the predecessors of the defendants as raiyats as ewll as bargadars are inconsistent and, therefore, such entries cannot raise any presumption in favour of the right of tenancy of the defendants predecessors. It seems to us that both the Courts below have failed to show proper appreciation of the claim of tenancy by a person who used to cultivate lands under the system known as barga. Although this question has been the subject for judicial exposition on several previous occasions, it appears to us that none of the Courts below have properly grasped the legal character of the relationship peculiar to such a system Both the Courts below appear to have proceeded on the view that a bargadar, that is a person cultivating certain land under the system known as barga cannot be a tenant as such, although he may claim or acquire such status under certain circumstances after abandoning his character of a bargadar. They have, therefore, thought that the entries in the record-of-rights showing an occupier of land to be a bargadar as well as a tenant are inconsistent and no legal presumption can be attached to such entries. They have in a similar way, taken the view that when the defendants stated that they were bargadars under the plaintiffs or their predecessors, it was an admission on their predecessors; it was an admission on their part that they have had no right of tenancy. 

 8. It has not been defined anywhere what a bargadar is we find in Wilson’s Glossaries, that the term barga has been defined as an agreement by which the cultivator engages to pay the landlord half of the produce, the latter providing half of the seed and paying the whole of the rent. From the definition of tenant as given in section 3, clause (17) of the Bengal Tenancy Act as it stood before the amendment of 1929, we find that a tenant means a person who holds land under another person and is or but for a special contract, would be liable to payment for that land to that person and in clause (13) of the same section, rent, has been defined as whatever is lawfully payable or deliverable in money or kind by a tenant to his landlord on account of the use or occupation of the land held by the tenant. So, we find that there is nothing in clause (13) or clause (17) of section 3 which militates against a bargadar being a tenant. Rent according to clause (13) of section 3, as we have seen, may be in money or in kind and it need not be a fixed amount, there is nothing in law to prevent a landlord from accepting a variable or fluctuating quantity of the produce of land as rent. Therefore, according to the provisions of law as were in force before 1929 there was nothing inherently inconsistent between the characters of a bargader and a tenant. Whether a bargadar has the character of a tenant or not depends upon the nature of the engagement between the landlord, i.e, the owner of the land and the bargadar who agrees to cultivate the lands on condition of delivering certain share of the produce of the land. If the intention of the parties is that a certain interest in land is to be demised by the transaction in question, then a right of tenancy will be created. But if, on the other hand, the intension is that the person who engages to cultivate the land would not acquire any interest in the land and would only cultivate it on the basis of certain remuneration which will be a share of the produce of the land then there will be no tenancy created in favour of the person. In one case, the intension of the parties is that there will be created an interest in favour of the occupier in respect of the land he cultivates and the owner of the land will receive a share of the produce by way of rent and in the other case no interest at all will be created in favour of the person cultivating the land, but he will receive a share of the crops grown by him by way of remuneration for the labour that he would devote for the cultivation of the land and growing the crops. So, it would always depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case whether a tenancy has been created or of a person on condition that he would cultivate it and give a certain share of the produce to the landlord. It was only in 1929 when by an amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the Legislature sought to bring about a certain change in regard to presumption about the status of a person who used to cultivate lands under barga system, by adding a proviso to the definition of “tenant” to section 3(17) of B.T. Act, which is to the following effect: 

 9. The legal implication of this proviso has been considered in a number of cases, more important of which may be noticed here. A Single Judge of the Dacca High Court (Hamoodur Rahman, J), as the learned Judge then was took the view on an interpretation of the proviso to section 3 (17) of the B T. Act, in the case of Abu Naser Sayedullah Vs Abdul Malik, reported in 12 DLR 206 same case PLD 1960 Dacca 587, that a bargadar was not nettled to put up a defence of his tenancy, in a suit for recovery of money on account of non-delivery of barga produce in respect of a period subsequent to the introduction of the Amending Act of 1929. Reliance was placed by the learned Single Judge on a decision of the Calcutta High Court reported as Sishumohan Koyal and others Vs. Rajendra Nath Sarcar and others In AIR 1938 Cal. 707. 

 12. As it has been pointed out by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that, even after the said amendment if a bargadar or adhiar or bhagdar has not been admitted as a tenant by a landlord nor has been adjudged a tenant by a Civil Court he can still raise a contention in any suit that he is a tenant and such a contention shall have to be decided on the basis of the evidence that may he adduced in that case It will appear from the judgment of the learned District Judge as well as from that of the learned Subordinate Judge who tried that quit, that they proceeded on the view that the term bargadar itself is a negation of the right of tenancy. The learned District Judge, at page 21 of the paper book after referring to the entries in Ext. A observed; 

 14. Apart from the question that it conceivable in law to have an occupancy right under another occupancy raiyat, although the status of the subordinate tenant will be that of an under rayiat, the learned District Judge seems to have made a mistake of fact in taking the view that the entries have no value because they purport to record one occupancy right under another occupancy right. This is not correct so far as the entries are concerned. As it will appear from Ext. 3 which is the superior khatian the record and owners have not been recorded as occupancy radials. It has been pointed out earlier, that there has been no entry in the column of 'Class of interest of the occupier' in the said khatian. Therefore, the ground which has weighed with the learned District Judge in inducing him to take the view that the defendants cannot claim to the right of tenancy because of the entries showing one occupancy right under another occupancy right has no basis. 

 15. The learned District Judge seems to have proceeded on the wrong view that the term bargadar is an antithesis of the term 'tenant' and that a person so long as he is a bargadar cannot claim a right of tenancy. The learned District Judge while assessing the evidence on record has therefore taken the view that when the defence witnesses have stated that the defendants were bargadars or that they delivered half of the crops to the plaintiffs or to plaintiffs predecessors, they have admitted that they had no right of tenancy, The learned District Jude, it appears to us was clearly in error in regard to his aforesaid approach to the evidence on record, and his endings have been vitiated as a result of want of proper appreciation of the real nature of the question involved. It may be pointed out that the same mistake was committed by the trial Court we are of the opinion that the judgment under appeal cannot be sustained. 

 16. Mr. Moinul Huq has also submitted that the Courts below have laid undue mess upon the recitals of Ext. 1 series, which, according to him, are not at all admissible against the contesting defendants of these documents Exts. 1 to 1 (b) and Ext. 2 are the documents of title of the plaintiffs. Ext. 1 (c) is a deed of transfer in favour of a third person in respect of the land of same khatian, and Exts. 1 (d) and 1 (e) are deeds of transfer in favour of the predecessors of the defendants in respect of the land of the same khatian. It is contended on behalf of the respondents that in these documents it has been clearly asserted that the recorded owners arc the owners in possession of these lands and the recitals disprove the claim of tenancy by the appellants. The Courts below proceeded also in the view that there are clear statements in these documents which belie the defence case. It may be pointed out that what has been asserted in all these documents is that the vendors or the executants having had raiyati right in the lands coveted by the respective transactions were owners in possession and for the facility of cultivation or management they were making the transfers. Strictly speaking the Courts below were not correct in their view that there was an assertion of occupancy right of khas possession in these documents. 

 18. It is to be pointed out that the plaintiffs case is that the plaintiffs predecessors had occupancy raiyati right in the disputed lands which they used to possess in khas and they had no subordinate tenants under them in respect of the suit lands, whereas the substantive defence case is that it was the defendant’s predecessors who, though bargadars had occupancy raiyati right in the said lands and had been possessing the same as such and the plaintiff’s predecessors were in the position of landlords realising barga produce the said lands. If the sale deeds, Ext 1 series and the patta Ext. 2 can be construed to mean that right of khas possession was sought to be transferred by the said deeds, then it can be reasonably contended that this right of khas possession was asserted by the plaintiffs predecessors by the said transaction, and they purpose of supporting the plaintiff’s case and disproving the defendants contention. The sale deeds Exts; 1(d) and 1(e), which are in not ipso facto demolish the defendants case, as had been supported by the Courts below and also strenuously argued by Mr Sobhan, the learned Advocate for the respondents. There is no incongruity between the existence of tenancy right of the defendants predecessors and their purchase of the superior right so as to absolve themselves from the obligation of payment of barga rent. If, however, the said documents, viz Exts 1(d) and 1(e) can be construed as asserting khas possession of the plaintiffs predecessors in the disputed khatian and transferring the same to the defendants predecessors, they will certainly be admissible in evidence in support of the plaintiffs case, as had been mentioned above, for the purpose of rebutting the presumption created by the C.S. record-of-rights. We, therefore, do not accept the contention of Mr. Moinul Huq that these documents are not admissible in evidence at all. 

 19. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents, has contended that the documentary evidence which has been adduced is sufficient to rebute the presumption if any, which may have been raised by the record-of-rights, Ext. A. as most of the documentary evidence are more than 30 years old and in this connection he has referred to the case reported in (1878) 3 Appeal Cases 644, pages 667 and 668 and (1899) 2 Chancery Division page 81. It may be ported but however, that both the Courts below have misconceived the character of the interest as evidenced by the entries in the record-or-rights and, as such, failed to consider the evidence from the correct standpoint. Because of this defect in the initial approach, the findings which have been arrived at, are not sustainable at all. The documents which have been proved by the plaintiff if they do actually prove the assertion or claim that the plaintiff had been possessing the lands in khas and that the defendants had no right of tenancy in the disputed land. 

 20. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan has drawn our attention to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case reported in 17 DLR (Supreme Court) 392 (which has already been referred to in another connection ) as to the presumption of correctness of a record-of-rights. It has been held in the said decision that the presumption of correctness of the record-of-rights if applicable only to the state of things as were existing at the time when the records were prepared, the further presumption that the same state of things has continued is under section 114 of the Evidence Act and the presumption of correctness of the record-of-rights weakens with the passage of time. It is true that in determining the question whether the defendants have got the tenancy right in the same may as their predecessors had, as recorded in the record-of-rights in the year, 1919, is based upon the second kind of presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act. But a Court of facts shall have to consider that, if the entry in the record-of-rights that the predecessors of the present defendants had tenancy right is presumed to have been correct at the time when the records were prepared, then the Court is also to satisfy itself that the said state of things was brought to an end in course of time by some other act or event. Therefore, in any view of matter, the evidence on record will have to be re-assessed attaching the necessary presumptive value to the said record or rights.
